title: Freelance Discovery Call Kit
description: Turn enquiries into well-priced proposals in one 25-minute call. Pre-call questionnaire, call script, 60-question bank, budget conversation scripts, a 10-point fit scorecard, six follow-up emails, a call tracker and a full worked example. Works in any doc app, Excel, Google Sheets or Numbers.

files.README.md:
# Freelance Discovery Call Kit

A discovery call is the 20–30 minute conversation between "a lead got in touch" and "I'm sending a proposal". Done well, it tells you whether the project is worth quoting, what it should cost, and what the client actually needs. Done badly, it turns into free consulting followed by a proposal that gets ghosted.

This kit gives you a repeatable system for every call.

## What's inside

| File | What it's for | When to use it |
|---|---|---|
| `pre-call-questionnaire.md` | Short form to send before you book | As soon as a lead replies |
| `call-script.md` | A 25-minute call structure with suggested wording | During the call |
| `question-bank.md` | 60 questions grouped by topic, plus what each answer tells you | Before the call, to pick 8–10 |
| `budget-talk-scripts.md` | How to raise money early without it feeling awkward | During the call |
| `fit-scorecard.md` | A 10-point scorecard to decide: propose, refer, or decline | Within an hour of the call |
| `follow-up-emails.md` | Six emails: confirm, recap, proposal intro, not-a-fit, no-show, chase | After the call |
| `discovery-call-tracker.csv` | Log every call and spot patterns | Weekly |
| `worked-example.md` | One full call, start to finish, for a fictional web designer | Read once first |

## How to use it (first time: about 45 minutes)

1. Read `worked-example.md` to see the whole flow.
2. Edit `pre-call-questionnaire.md` so the questions fit your service. Paste it into an email, a doc, or your form tool of choice.
3. Pick 8–10 questions from `question-bank.md` and add them to section 3 of `call-script.md`. Keep the rest for later.
4. Write your own version of one budget script from `budget-talk-scripts.md` and say it out loud three times. It gets easier.
5. Open `discovery-call-tracker.csv` in Excel, Google Sheets or Numbers and delete the sample rows when you're ready.

## Every call after that (about 10 minutes of admin)

- Before: send the questionnaire, read the answers, skim their website.
- During: follow the script, take notes in the scorecard headings.
- After: score the call, send the recap email the same day, log it in the tracker.

## Three rules that make this work

1. **Talk about money in the first half of the call.** If the budget doesn't fit, you both find out in minute 10, not after you've spent two hours on a proposal.
2. **Diagnose, don't solve.** Ask about the problem, the cost of the problem, and what success looks like. Save the how for the paid work.
3. **Always end with a next step and a date.** "I'll send a proposal by Thursday; can we book 15 minutes on Friday to go through it?"

All templates are plain text. Replace anything in [square brackets].

# Worked example: one discovery call, start to finish

A fictional freelance web designer, Sam, gets an enquiry from a fictional business, Harbour Bakery. Here's how the kit is used at each step.

## Day 1, 10:05: the enquiry

> "Hi, we need a new website. Ours is old. How much would that cost?" — Priya, Harbour Bakery

Sam doesn't quote. Sam replies with the pre-call questionnaire email.

## Day 1, 16:40: the questionnaire comes back

- **What do you want to get done?** New website, easier to update, with online cake orders.
- **Why now?** Opening a second shop in March. Phone orders are taking two hours a day.
- **Great result in six months?** Most custom-cake orders come in online. Staff stop answering the phone during the morning rush.
- **Tried before?** A nephew built the current site in 2019. Nobody can edit it.
- **Deadline?** Live by 1 March, before the new shop opens.
- **Decision?** Priya and her business partner, Tom.
- **Budget?** 3,000–6,000.

Sam's read: real trigger (new shop), clear pain (two hours a day on the phone), fixed date, budget fits. Book the call. Ask for Tom to join.

## Day 3: the call (Sam's notes, under the scorecard headings)

**Problem:** It's not really "the site is old". It's that custom cake orders arrive by phone, need a back-and-forth about size and flavour, and get written on paper. Two missed orders last month.

**Impact:** About 2 staff hours a day on the phone, roughly 10 hours a week. Two missed orders in December worth about 180 each. With a second shop the problem doubles.

**Budget:** Sam used the range anchor script: "Sites like this with an order form usually run from about 3,500 for a lean version to 6,500 with online payment and a full menu." Tom: "We'd thought about 5,000, but if online payment saves the phone calls, we could stretch." Budget: 5,000, flexible to about 6,000.

**Timeline:** Live by 1 March, fixed. Content (photos, menu) ready by mid-January. Feedback within 2 days, Priya decides day to day, Tom signs off spend.

**Decision:** Priya and Tom, both on the call. Talking to one other designer. Will decide within a week of the proposal.

Questions Sam picked from the bank: 2, 3, 8, 10, 17, 29, 33, 34, 36, 43.

Best answer of the call, to question 43 ("What went well or badly with freelancers before?"): "The nephew never told us when things would be done." Sam writes "weekly Friday update" straight into the proposal.

**Next step:** Sam proposes three options, and they book a review call for Day 6 before hanging up.

## Day 3, after the call: the scorecard

| # | Question | Score |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Problem clear | 2 |
| 2 | Impact justifies cost | 2 |
| 3 | Budget vs. price | 2 |
| 4 | Timeline vs. capacity | 1 (tight in February) |
| 5 | Decision maker | 2 |
| 6 | Skills | 2 |
| 7 | Client readiness | 1 (photos not shot yet) |
| 8 | Communication | 2 |
| 9 | Portfolio value | 2 |
| 10 | Gut | 1 |
| | **Total** | **17/20** |

Red flags: none. Decision: propose.

## Day 3, 17:30: the recap email

> **Where things are now:** Custom cake orders come in by phone and are written on paper, taking about 10 staff hours a week, with two missed orders last month.
> **Why it matters:** The second shop opens in March and will double the phone volume.
> **What success looks like:** Most custom orders placed online, with the details you need captured in one go.
> **Timing:** Live by 1 March. Photos and menu ready by mid-January.
> **Budget:** Around 5,000, with room to go further if online payment is included.

## Day 4: the proposal

Three options, anchored on what the call uncovered:

1. **Lean, 3,600:** new 5-page site and a structured cake order form that emails the shop.
2. **Standard, 5,200 (recommended):** as above, plus deposit payment at order time and an automatic confirmation email to the customer.
3. **Complete, 6,400:** as standard, plus a separate page and order flow for each shop.

## Day 6: the review call

Priya and Tom chose Standard and asked to add the second shop page later. Signed on Day 7.

## What made the difference

- The questionnaire turned "how much for a website?" into a real brief before any call.
- Asking about impact (question 8) gave Sam the "10 hours a week" figure, which made 5,200 look reasonable.
- Budget came up in minute 11, so nobody wasted time on a wrong-sized proposal.
- The review call was booked during the discovery call.
- The recap email let Tom sign off without needing another meeting.

# Pre-call questionnaire

Send this before you book the call. It filters out tyre-kickers, saves 10 minutes of the call, and shows the client you're organised. Keep it to 6–8 questions: long forms get abandoned.

## Email to send with it

> Subject: Quick questions before we talk
>
> Hi [Name],
>
> Thanks for getting in touch about [project]. So I can make our call useful rather than spending it on basics, could you answer the short questions below? It takes about five minutes.
>
> Once I have your answers I'll send a link to book a 25-minute call.
>
> [Your name]

## The questions

1. **In a sentence or two, what do you want to get done?**
2. **Why now?** What's prompting this project at the moment?
3. **What does a great result look like six months after the project is finished?**
4. **Have you tried to solve this before?** If so, what happened?
5. **When do you need it finished, and is that date fixed?** (e.g. a launch, an event, a funding deadline)
6. **Who else is involved in the decision?**
7. **What budget range have you set aside?**
   - Under [£/$/€ X]
   - [X] – [Y]
   - [Y] – [Z]
   - Over [Z]
   - Not sure yet, and I'd like guidance
8. **Anything else I should know?** (links, examples you like, constraints)

## How to set your budget bands

Use your real prices. If your smallest worthwhile project is 1,500, make the bands something like: under 1,500 / 1,500–3,000 / 3,000–6,000 / over 6,000. Anyone who picks "under 1,500" gets a polite note pointing them to a cheaper option (see `follow-up-emails.md`, email 4) instead of a call.

## Reading the answers

| Signal | What it usually means |
|---|---|
| Clear "why now" with a date attached | Real project with urgency. Prioritise. |
| "Just exploring" / no date | Early stage. Offer a call, but don't build a custom proposal yet. |
| Budget band matches your pricing | Book the call. |
| Budget "not sure" | Fine. Use a budget script on the call. |
| Budget well below your range | Send the not-a-fit email with a referral. |
| Several decision makers, only one on the form | Ask for the decision maker to join the call. |
| Answers are one word each | Low commitment. Short call, or ask one follow-up question by email first. |

# 25-minute discovery call script

You don't need to read this word for word. Use the structure and the time boxes; put the wording in your own voice.

Keep notes under the five headings from `fit-scorecard.md`: Problem, Impact, Budget, Timeline, Decision.

---

## 1. Open and set the agenda (2 minutes)

> "Thanks for making the time. I've read your answers, so I'd like to use this call to understand the project properly. I'll ask a lot of questions for about 15 minutes, then tell you how I'd approach it and what it would roughly cost. At the end we can decide together whether a proposal makes sense. Does that work?"

Why: it tells the client you'll lead, that money will come up, and that "no" is an acceptable outcome. That lowers pressure on both sides.

## 2. The problem and why now (5 minutes)

> "You mentioned [their answer to question 1]. Can you tell me more about what's happening today?"
> "What made this a priority now rather than six months ago?"
> "What have you already tried?"

Listen for: the real problem behind the requested deliverable. "We need a new website" is often "our enquiries dropped and we don't know why".

## 3. Impact and success (5 minutes)

Use 2–4 questions you picked from `question-bank.md`. Always include one of these:

> "If this goes really well, what's different in six months?"
> "What happens if you don't do this project at all?"

Why: the size of the impact is what justifies your price. A problem costing them 2,000 a month makes a 5,000 fix look sensible.

## 4. Budget (3 minutes)

Use a script from `budget-talk-scripts.md`. Do this before you talk about your approach.

## 5. Timeline and decision (3 minutes)

> "When do you need this live, and what's driving that date?"
> "Apart from you, who needs to say yes? Is there anything that would stop this going ahead?"
> "How will you decide between options?"

## 6. Your approach, at a high level (4 minutes)

Summarise what you heard, then give the outline, not the detailed plan:

> "So what I'm hearing is: [problem], it's costing you [impact], and success means [outcome] by [date]. The way I'd approach that is in three stages: [stage 1], [stage 2], [stage 3]. Projects like this usually land between [X] and [Y]."

If they say "that's more than we thought", go to the "budget is lower than your price" section of `budget-talk-scripts.md`.

## 7. Agree the next step (3 minutes)

> "Here's what I suggest: I'll send a short proposal by [day] with two options. Can we book 15 minutes on [day] to go through it together?"

Book that second call while you're still on this one. Proposals reviewed live close far more often than proposals sent and left.

If it's not a fit, say so kindly now:

> "Honestly, based on the budget and timeline, I don't think I'm the right person for this. I'll send you the names of a couple of people who might be. Is that OK?"

---

## After the call (10 minutes)

1. Score it in `fit-scorecard.md`.
2. Send the recap email (`follow-up-emails.md`, email 2) the same day.
3. Add a row to `discovery-call-tracker.csv`.
files.question-bank.md:
# Question bank

Pick 8–10 for each call. Don't ask them all. Each question has a note on what the answer tells you.

## The problem

1. What's happening today that made you reach out? — *The trigger. Real projects have one.*
2. How long has this been a problem? — *Long-standing problems may have hidden blockers.*
3. What have you already tried? What happened? — *Tells you what not to propose, and whether a previous freelancer left a mess.*
4. If you had to describe the problem to a colleague in one sentence, what would you say? — *Cuts through jargon.*
5. Who feels this problem most? — *Often not the person on the call.*
6. What's the part of this you're most worried about? — *The risk you need to address in the proposal.*
7. Is this one problem or several tied together? — *Scope warning.*

## Impact and value

8. What does this problem cost you right now, in time or money? — *Anchors your price against value.*
9. If nothing changes, what happens in a year? — *Urgency.*
10. What would success look like six months after we finish? — *Your success criteria for the proposal.*
11. How will you measure whether it worked? — *If they can't say, help them; otherwise expect "it doesn't feel right" feedback later.*
12. What would it mean for you personally if this goes well? — *The emotional driver. Use gently.*
13. Which matters most: speed, quality, or cost? You can pick two. — *Shapes your options.*

## Scope

14. What's definitely in this project? — *Core deliverables.*
15. What's definitely not in it? — *Boundaries. Write these into the proposal.*
16. What do you already have that I can use? (content, brand files, data, access) — *Hidden work lives here.*
17. Who will provide [content / data / feedback], and by when? — *Client-side delays are the top cause of overruns.*
18. Are there other people or agencies I'd be working alongside? — *Coordination time.*
19. What happens after launch? Who looks after it? — *Possible ongoing work, or a handover need.*
20. Are there examples you like, and what do you like about them? — *Taste and expectations.*
21. Anything you've seen that you definitely don't want? — *Faster than guessing.*

## Budget

22. Have you set a budget for this? — *Simple and direct.*
23. What range did you have in mind? — *If they won't say a number.*
24. Is that budget fixed, or could it flex for the right result? — *Room for an upper option.*
25. Is the budget for this phase only, or the whole thing? — *Avoids a nasty surprise.*
26. How have you paid freelancers or agencies before: fixed fee, day rate, retainer? — *Their expectations.*
27. When does the budget need to be spent or committed? — *Fiscal-year deadlines create urgency.*

## Timeline

28. When do you need this finished? — *Obvious, but ask.*
29. What's driving that date? — *Fixed (event, launch) vs. preferred.*
30. What happens if it slips by two weeks? — *How hard the deadline really is.*
31. When would you want to start? — *Check your capacity.*
32. Are there any dates when you or your team aren't available? — *Holidays kill feedback rounds.*
33. How quickly can you usually give feedback? — *Two days vs. two weeks changes the schedule.*

## Decision

34. Who else is involved in deciding? — *Find the real decision maker.*
35. What would they need to see to say yes? — *Write the proposal for them.*
36. Are you talking to anyone else about this? — *Competition. It's fine to ask.*
37. How will you choose? — *Their criteria; address each one.*
38. Is there anything that could stop this going ahead? — *Hidden objections.*
39. If my proposal looks right, how soon could you decide? — *Sets your follow-up schedule.*
40. What's the approval process for paying a new supplier? — *Purchase orders, supplier forms, payment runs.*

## Working together

41. How do you prefer to communicate: email, calls, a chat tool? — *Avoid friction early.*
42. How often would you like updates? — *Set expectations.*
43. What went well or badly with freelancers you've worked with before? — *Gold. Do the good things; avoid the bad.*
44. How involved do you want to be day to day? — *Hands-on clients need more check-ins; price for it.*
45. Who will be my main contact? — *One voice for feedback.*

## Fit (ask yourself, not them)

46. Do I understand the problem well enough to explain it back?
47. Can I deliver a great result within the budget?
48. Do I have capacity on their timeline?
49. Would I be happy to show this work in my portfolio?
50. Did anything in the call worry me?

## Useful follow-ups for any answer

51. "Can you say more about that?"
52. "What do you mean by [their word]?"
53. "Why is that important?"
54. "Can you give me an example?"
55. "What else?"
56. "How would you know?"
57. "If you could only fix one thing, which would it be?"
58. "What would make you say this was a waste of money?"
59. "Is there anything I haven't asked that I should have?"
60. "What's the best way to reach you if I have questions while writing the proposal?"

## Questions to avoid

- **"What's your budget?" as your first question.** Earn it with 10 minutes of interest first.
- **"Would you like me to do X?"** Too easy to say yes; it inflates scope. Ask what they need.
- **Leading questions** like "You'd want it mobile friendly, right?" Ask "Where will people mostly use this?"
- **Solving live.** If you catch yourself designing the solution, stop and ask another question.
files.budget-talk-scripts.md:
# Budget talk scripts

Most freelancers avoid the budget question, then spend hours on proposals the client could never afford. These scripts make it routine. Say the money part plainly and then stop talking. Silence is fine.

## When to raise it

After you understand the problem and its impact (around minute 10–12), and before you describe your approach. If you describe the approach first, you're designing for free.

---

## Script 1: The direct ask

> "Do you have a budget in mind for this?"

Then wait. Most clients will give you a number or a range.

## Script 2: The range anchor (when they won't name a number)

> "That's fine, a lot of people don't. To give you a sense: projects like this typically run between [X] for a lean version and [Y] for the fuller version we talked about. Where does that sit with what you were expecting?"

Why it works: you've given a real reference point, and they only have to react, which is much easier than naming a number.

## Script 3: The three-tier check

> "I usually see three ways to do this. A focused version at around [X] that solves [the core problem]. A standard version around [Y] that also covers [extra]. And a complete version around [Z] with [extra]. Which of those feels closest?"

Use this when the scope is still loose. Their answer tells you what to put in the proposal.

## Script 4: When they ask your price before you're ready

> "Happy to talk numbers, and I will before we finish. I just don't want to guess before I understand what you need, because I'd either quote too high and scare you off, or too low and have to come back later. Can I ask a few more questions first?"

## Script 5: When the budget is lower than your price

Don't drop your price straight away. Reduce the scope instead.

> "Thanks for being upfront. With [their budget], I couldn't do everything we've discussed and do it well. What I could do is [smaller scope that solves the most important part]. Then we can look at [the rest] later. Would that work?"

If even the smallest useful version doesn't fit:

> "I don't think I can do a good job at that budget, and I'd rather tell you now than waste your time. I can recommend a couple of people who work in that range, if that helps."

## Script 6: When the budget is much higher than expected

Don't say "great, that's plenty". Ask what else matters.

> "That gives us room to do this properly. Is there anything you'd want included at that level, like [ongoing support / extra deliverable / faster turnaround]?"

## Script 7: When someone else holds the budget

> "Who signs off on the spend? It might be worth a quick chat with them before I write the proposal, so I can make sure it answers their questions too."

## Script 8: Day rate vs. fixed fee

> "I usually price projects like this as a fixed fee, so you know the total cost before we start. Changes outside the agreed scope are quoted separately before I do them. Does that suit how you work?"

---

## Practise these

Pick the two you'll use most. Write them in your own words. Say them out loud until they sound normal. The first few times will feel awkward; by the tenth call you won't notice.

## Common mistakes

- **Apologising.** "Sorry, I have to ask about money…" signals that money is uncomfortable. It's a normal business question.
- **Filling the silence.** After you say a number, stop. Let them respond.
- **Discounting on the call.** Never cut price live. Say you'll look at options and put them in the proposal.
- **Quoting a single number.** A range or three tiers lets them choose instead of just accepting or rejecting.
files.fit-scorecard.md:
# Fit scorecard

Fill this in within an hour of the call, while it's fresh. It turns a gut feeling into a clear decision: propose, propose with conditions, refer, or decline.

## Call notes

**Client / company:** [ ]
**Date of call:** [ ]
**Project in one sentence:** [ ]

**Problem** (what's really going on):
[ ]

**Impact** (what it costs them, what success looks like):
[ ]

**Budget** (number or range, fixed or flexible):
[ ]

**Timeline** (date needed, and why):
[ ]

**Decision** (who decides, how, by when):
[ ]

## Score it

Give each line 0, 1 or 2 points.

| # | Question | 0 points | 1 point | 2 points | Score |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Is the problem clear? | Vague, keeps changing | Mostly clear | Clear and specific | |
| 2 | Does the impact justify the cost? | Not really | Probably | Clearly | |
| 3 | Budget vs. your price | Below your minimum | Within 20% | At or above | |
| 4 | Timeline vs. your capacity | Can't do it | Tight but possible | Comfortable | |
| 5 | Decision maker | Unknown | Known, not on the call | On the call | |
| 6 | Your skills | Stretch | Good fit | Bread and butter | |
| 7 | Client readiness (content, access, feedback) | Nothing ready | Some | Ready to go | |
| 8 | Communication on the call | Difficult | Fine | Easy, respectful | |
| 9 | Portfolio or referral value | None | Some | High | |
| 10 | Your gut feeling | Uneasy | Neutral | Excited | |
| | **Total** | | | | **/20** |

## Decide

| Score | Action |
|---|---|
| **16–20** | Write the proposal. Send it within two working days. |
| **11–15** | Propose, but deal with the weak lines first. E.g. low budget: offer a smaller scope; decision maker absent: ask for a 15-minute call with them. |
| **6–10** | Usually refer elsewhere. Only propose if you have a specific reason (quiet month, strategic client), and price for the risk. |
| **0–5** | Decline politely (`follow-up-emails.md`, email 4). |

**Any 0 on line 3, 4 or 8?** Treat that as a red flag whatever the total. A client you can't afford to work for, can't fit in, or can't talk to is rarely worth it.

## Red flags worth writing down

Tick any you noticed. Two or more: think hard before proposing.

- [ ] Asked for free sample work or a "test project"
- [ ] Criticised every previous freelancer at length
- [ ] Wanted a firm quote before explaining the project
- [ ] Deadline is "yesterday" with no clear reason
- [ ] Refused to discuss budget at all, even as a range
- [ ] Scope grew noticeably during the call
- [ ] Pushed for a discount before seeing a proposal
- [ ] "It should be quick, it's really simple"
- [ ] Missed or was very late to the call without a message

## Decision

**Outcome:** Propose / Propose with conditions / Refer / Decline
**Next step and date:** [ ]
**Proposal options to include:** [ ]
files.follow-up-emails.md:
# Follow-up emails

Six emails covering everything from booking to "it's not a fit". Copy, adjust to your voice, and replace anything in [square brackets].

---

## 1. Booking confirmation (send when the call is booked)

> Subject: Confirmed: our call on [day, date]
>
> Hi [Name],
>
> Looking forward to talking on [day, date] at [time, time zone]. [Call link or phone number.]
>
> I've read your answers. To make the most of our 25 minutes, it would help if you could have to hand:
> - [Any examples you like / current analytics / the brief]
> - The name of anyone else who'll be involved in the decision (they're welcome to join)
>
> If anything changes, just reply to this email.
>
> [Your name]

---

## 2. Recap (send the same day as the call)

The most important email in the kit. It shows you listened, confirms what you'll quote for, and gives them something to forward to the decision maker.

> Subject: Recap of our call + next steps
>
> Hi [Name],
>
> Thanks for your time today. Here's what I took away, so you can tell me if I've missed anything:
>
> **Where things are now:** [the problem in their words]
> **Why it matters:** [the impact: time, money, opportunity]
> **What success looks like:** [the outcome and how you'll measure it]
> **Timing:** [date and what's driving it]
> **Budget:** [the range discussed]
>
> **Next steps**
> 1. I'll send a proposal with [two/three] options by [day].
> 2. We're booked for [day, time] to go through it together.
>
> If I've got any of this wrong, just reply and I'll adjust before I write the proposal.
>
> [Your name]

---

## 3. Proposal cover email

> Subject: Proposal for [project]
>
> Hi [Name],
>
> As promised, here's my proposal for [project]. [Attached / link.]
>
> In short: I've included [number] options, from [lowest option, price] to [highest option, price]. Based on what you told me about [their key priority], I'd recommend [option], because [one-sentence reason].
>
> We're booked for [day, time] to talk it through. If you'd like to share it with [decision maker] before then, it's written so it makes sense on its own.
>
> [Your name]

---

## 4. Not a fit (with a referral)

Send this when the budget, timing or type of work doesn't match. Be kind and quick; people remember freelancers who were honest with them, and some come back later with a bigger project.

> Subject: Re: [project]
>
> Hi [Name],
>
> Thanks for telling me about [project]. Having thought about it, I don't think I'm the right fit, mainly because [budget / timeline / type of work], and I'd rather say so now than send a proposal that doesn't work for you.
>
> A couple of suggestions that might help:
> - [Name or type of provider], who [why they suit this]
> - [A cheaper or DIY option, if appropriate]
>
> If your plans change or you have a project that's more [your specialty] in future, I'd be glad to hear from you.
>
> All the best with it,
> [Your name]

---

## 5. No-show

Assume good faith once. If they no-show twice, let it go.

> Subject: Sorry we missed each other
>
> Hi [Name],
>
> I was on the call at [time] but didn't see you. No problem, these things happen.
>
> If you'd still like to talk, here's my booking link again: [link]. Or just reply with a couple of times that suit you.
>
> [Your name]

---

## 6. Proposal chase (if they go quiet)

Send 3 working days after the proposal if you didn't get a review call, then once more a week later. After that, move them to "closed – no response" in your tracker.

**First chase**

> Subject: Re: Proposal for [project]
>
> Hi [Name],
>
> Just checking the proposal reached you safely. Do you have any questions, or would a quick 10-minute call help?
>
> [Your name]

**Second and final chase**

> Subject: Re: Proposal for [project]
>
> Hi [Name],
>
> I don't want to fill your inbox, so this is my last nudge. If the timing isn't right or you've gone another way, no problem at all; a one-line reply would help me plan my schedule.
>
> I'm holding [start date] for now and will release it on [date].
>
